grammar.heading: c1-1-7-a-no-b
grammar.quote: A noun phrase is built by joining two or more nouns with a marker: noun no noun means "noun of noun" or "noun's noun", noun to noun means "noun and noun", and noun ka noun means "noun or noun". The marker no is a modifier or possessive marker. It covers belonging (my office), relationship (the president of ADZ) and description (a Japanese language student). The main noun comes last, and you can stack more than one no in a row. A sentence can also end with no to mean "A's one", as in kono kuruma wa ana san no desu.

grammar.heading: c3-3-7-counters
grammar.quote: In Japanese you do not just say "three apples". You add a counter, which is a short ending that depends on what you are counting. This chapter teaches tsu (anything), sai (age), nin (people), mai (thin, flat things), hon (long, thin things), satsu (books and notebooks), kai (times), kai (floors of a building), ko (small things), hiki (small animals), dai (machines and vehicles) and ban or banme (order, such as which child you are). Pages use the counter pe-ji. The number and the counter join into one word: san plus ko is sanko.

grammar.heading: c6-6-6-i-adjectives-present-past-and-negati
grammar.quote: With i-adjectives, the adjective itself changes for negative and past, and desu stays as the polite ending. Take the final i off and add kunai for the negative, katta for the past, and kunakatta for the past negative. So takai (expensive) gives takakunai (not expensive), takakatta (was expensive) and takakunakatta (was not expensive).

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-6-i-adjectives-present-past-and-negati
grammarRules.quote: The book writes desu in brackets in its tables, because it can be dropped in casual speech. This whole book uses the polite style, so keep desu: takakatta desu. Do not change desu to deshita after an i-adjective. Takai deshita is wrong, and takakatta desu is right.

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-6-i-adjectives-present-past-and-negati
grammarRules.quote: Ii (good) is the only irregular adjective. It cannot be conjugated, so its other form yoi takes over: yokunai (not good), yokatta (was good) and yokunakatta (was not good). Never say iikunai or iikatta. Also watch tsumaranai (boring). It ends in nai, but it is a normal i-adjective, so its negative is tsumaranakunai (not boring), and its past is tsumaranakatta.

grammar.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk
grammar.quote: The second job of an adjective is to connect to another adjective, as in big and heavy. The first adjective changes shape, and the last one keeps its normal form.

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk
grammarRules.quote: The second job of an adjective is to connect to another adjective, as in big and heavy. The first adjective changes shape, and the last one keeps its normal form.

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk
grammarRules.quote: With an i-adjective, drop the final i and add kute: atarashii becomes atarashikute, so atarashikute takai means new and expensive. With a na-adjective, drop the na and add de: nigiyaka(na) becomes nigiyaka de, so nigiyaka de rippa na means lively and splendid. The same chains work in front of a noun, as in atsukute omoi hon (a thick, heavy book). When the last adjective is a na-adjective in front of a noun, it keeps its na: kirei de shizuka na tokoro (a clean, quiet place).

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk
grammarRules.quote: Only the last adjective carries desu and the tense. Say kono heya wa akarukute hiroi desu for This room is bright and wide, and put only the last word in the past: akarukute hirokatta desu. Ii (good) uses its other form here: yokute yasui means good and cheap.

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk
grammarRules.quote: In practice, join qualities that go together in mood, such as akarukute hiroi (bright and wide) or muzukashikute tsumaranai (difficult and boring). Joining a good point with a bad point needs a different word, which this chapter does not cover.

grammar.heading: c6-6-10-a-little-and-not-very-chotto-and-am
grammar.quote: Chotto means a little. Put it in front of an adjective, and the adjective keeps its normal form: chotto semai desu (it is a little small). Chotto also makes a refusal sound soft. Sumimasen, ima chotto isogashii desu is a polite way to say you cannot do something now.

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-10-a-little-and-not-very-chotto-and-am

Say amari takakunai desu (not very expensive) or amari kantan ja arimasen (not very easy), and never amari takai desu. It works in the past as well: amari muzukashikunakatta desu (it was not very difficult).

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-10-a-little-and-not-very-chotto-and-am

grammarRules.heading: c7-7-2-time-expression-ni-verb-bunkei-7-1

grammarRules.heading: c7-7-1-verbs-in-the-formal-form-masu-masen-

grammarRules.heading: c7-7-1-verbs-in-the-formal-form-masu-masen-

The time word in the sentence tells you which one is meant. grammarRules.heading: c7-7-1-verbs-in-the-formal-form-masu-masen-
grammarRules.quote: Umaremasu (be born) is in the word list, but the workbook never uses it. Because being born has already happened, you will mostly meet it in the past: umaremashita. grammarRules.heading: c9-9-10-from-masu-form-to-dictionary-form-p
grammarRules.quote: For Irregular verbs, change the last sound of the stem from the i row to the u row. Nomi becomes nomu, and kaki becomes kaku. grammarRules.heading: c9-9-10-from-masu-form-to-dictionary-form-p

grammarRules.heading: c9-9-1-destination-e-or-ni-and-origin-kara-

grammarRules.heading: c9-9-1-destination-e-or-ni-and-origin-kara-

grammarRules.heading: c9-9-1-destination-e-or-ni-and-origin-kara-

grammarRules.heading: c7-7-7-i-adjective-as-an-adverb-bunkei-7-6

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk
grammarRules.quote: With an i-adjective, drop the final i and add kute: atarashii becomes atarashikute, so atarashikute takai means new and expensive. With a na-adjective, drop the na and add de: nigiyaka(na) becomes nigiyaka de, so nigiyaka de rippa na means lively and splendid. When the last adjective is a na-adjective in front of a noun, it keeps its na: kirei de shizuka na tokoro (a clean, quiet place).

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk

grammarRules.heading: c6-6-5-adjective-adjective-kute-and-de-bunk

grammarRules.heading: c10-10-21-informal-desu-and-informal-adjecti

grammarRules.heading: c10-10-21-informal-desu-and-informal-adjecti

grammar.heading: c10-10-11-masen-to-the-nai-form-present-nega
grammar.quote: To make the informal present negative, change the verb to its nai form. The rule depends on the group. For Group 1 to Group 5, the final u sound changes to the a sound and nai is added (nomu becomes nomanai, kau becomes kawanai). For Regular verbs, drop ru and add nai (taberu becomes tabenai). For Special verbs, suru becomes shinai and kuru becomes konai.

grammarRules.heading: c10-10-13-masen-deshita-to-the-nakatta-form-

grammarRules.heading: c10-10-13-masen-deshita-to-the-nakatta-form-
